q: Which architect designed the Eigen Haard Estate in Amsterdam (1920)?
n: Michel de Klerk designed Eigen Haard. He is also the expressionist co-designer of the Scheepvaarthuis in the same city.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous Examples of Social Housing

q: Walter Gropius designed the Bauhaus Complex in Dessau (1925) and which later New York building (1963)?
n: Gropius's New York building is the MetLife Building (1963). The Seagram Building is by Mies van der Rohe and Philip Johnson.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Bauhaus Style Architects

q: In what year did Mies van der Rohe succeed Hannes Meyer as director of the Bauhaus?
n: Mies took over from Meyer in 1930. 1933 is when the Bauhaus period ends, and 1925 is when Gropius built the Dessau complex.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Bauhaus Style Architects

q: In the United States, Bauhaus ideas were developed by Walter Gropius, Mies van der Rohe, and which other European emigrant?
n: Richard Neutra is named with Gropius and Mies. Le Corbusier stayed in France and is not part of that American group.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Bauhaus Design School

q: Who designed the Karl Marx Hof in Vienna (1930)?
n: Karl Ehn (1884–1957) designed the Karl Marx Hof, the Vienna entry on the social housing list. Loos and Olbrich are Viennese architects from other movements.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous Examples of Social Housing

q: The Bauhaus combined several sources. Which is NOT one of them?
n: The Bauhaus drew on Constructivism, De Stijl, and Frank Lloyd Wright. Floral ornament is the opposite of its deliberate absence of decoration.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Bauhaus Design School

q: Minimal-cost social housing projects in major urban centres were a response to what?
o: Bomb damage after World War II
The European post-war housing crisis of the 1920s
n: The projects answered the 1920s housing crisis in Europe after World War I, which is why the movement ends around 1930.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Social Housing Architecture

q: The Bauhaus attitude to crafts was modelled on which two movements?
o: Arts & Crafts and the Deutscher Werkbund
Art Nouveau and the Vienna Secession
n: The crafts attitude came from the Arts & Crafts movement and the Deutscher Werkbund. De Stijl influenced the Bauhaus too, but in form rather than crafts.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Bauhaus Design School

q: What date range does the movements table give for the Bauhaus Design School?
n: The Bauhaus ran from 1919 to 1933, when the school closed. The range 1918–1930 is Social Housing.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Bauhaus Design School

q: On the European continent, social housing of the 1920s mostly took what form?
n: Continental social housing was built as large-scale apartment blocks, such as Vienna's Karl Marx Hof.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Social Housing Architecture

q: The Works Housing Estate at Hoek van Holland (1924) was designed by whom?
n: J.J.P. Oud designed the Hoek van Holland estate, in keeping with his role as Rotterdam's municipal housing architect.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous Examples of Social Housing

q: The Bruchfeldstrasse Estate in Frankfurt am Main (1927) was designed by whom?
n: Ernst May (1886–1970) designed the Bruchfeldstrasse Estate as part of his housing work in Frankfurt.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous Examples of Social Housing

q: Le Corbusier's contribution to 1920s social housing was the estate at which place?
n: Le Corbusier designed the Pessac Housing Estate near Bordeaux (1926), the one French example on the list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous Examples of Social Housing

q: Siemensstadt in Berlin (1929) was designed by which architect, with others?
n: Hans Scharoun (1893–1972) and others designed Siemensstadt. Taut's Berlin estate is the Britz Horseshoe.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous Examples of Social Housing

q: Which Swiss Marxist was professor of architecture and later director at the Bauhaus?
n: Hannes Meyer (1889–1954) was the Swiss Marxist who became director. Mies van der Rohe succeeded him.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Bauhaus Style Architects

q: What date range does the movements table give for Social Housing Architecture?
n: Social Housing Architecture is dated 1918–30, the post-World War I decade. The range 1919–1933 is the Bauhaus.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Social Housing Architecture

q: László Moholy-Nagy taught the Bauhaus Vorkurs and later directed the New Bauhaus in which city?
n: Moholy-Nagy directed the New Bauhaus in Chicago (1937–8). Dessau was the original Bauhaus's second home, not the new school.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Bauhaus Style Architects

q: Bauhaus design, with its clean lines and deliberate lack of ornament, eventually developed into what?
o: The International Style of modern architecture
n: The Bauhaus led into the International Style, which then spread to the US. Expressionism came earlier and rebelled against exactly this kind of plain functionalism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Bauhaus Design School

q: How did the Bauhaus design ethos reach the United States?
o: Through key teaching staff who emigrated there in the 1930s
Through a travelling exhibition sent by the German government
Through a manifesto published in American journals
Through American students who studied in Weimar
n: The Bauhaus ethos was carried by teaching staff who moved to the US in the 1930s, including Gropius, Mies van der Rohe, and Moholy-Nagy.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Bauhaus Design School

q: Who designed the Britz Horseshoe Estate in Berlin (1925–33)?
n: Bruno Taut designed the Horseshoe Estate at Britz. Scharoun is the other Berlin name on the list, for Siemensstadt.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous Examples of Social Housing

q: Which architect is credited with the Weissenhofsiedlung in Stuttgart (1927)?
n: The table credits the Weissenhofsiedlung to Mies van der Rohe. Oud and Le Corbusier took part in the exhibition, but Mies is the name listed for the estate.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous Examples of Social Housing

q: When and where did Deconstructivism notably emerge?
n: Deconstructivism emerged in the 1980s, notably in Los Angeles, and also appeared in Europe. Gehry, its best-known American figure, was based in LA.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Deconstructivism

q: Which building by James Stirling is cited as a demonstration of the high-tech approach?
o: The glass Engineering Faculty, Leicester University
n: Stirling's glass Engineering Faculty at Leicester University (1959–63) is the example. Lloyd's is Richard Rogers and the Sage Gateshead is Norman Foster.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: High-Tech Architecture

q: The exhibition that first introduced Deconstructivism to the public was held where, and when?
o: The Museum of Modern Art, New York, in 1988
n: The Deconstructivist Architecture exhibition was held at MoMA, New York, in 1988. Expo 67 is the exhibition tied to high-tech.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Deconstructivism

q: The Hong Kong and Shanghai Bank in Hong Kong (1979–86) was designed by which firm?
n: Foster & Partners designed the Hong Kong and Shanghai Bank. SOM is known on these pages for the Inland Steel Building and Fazlur Khan's tube structures.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous High-Tech Buildings

q: The Olympiapark in Munich (1968–72) was designed by Günter Behnisch and whom?
n: Behnisch worked with Frei Otto on the Olympiapark. Herzog & de Meuron built Munich's later Allianz Arena (2005).
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous High-Tech Buildings

q: What gives a deconstructivist building its unpredictable, even shocking, appearance?
o: Non-rectilinear shapes that distort the structure's geometry
Organic bulging forms made of plastic panels
Austere right angles in primary colours
n: Non-rectilinear shapes that distort geometry create the deconstructivist look. Bulging organic forms describe blobitecture, a close relative.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Deconstructivism

q: Deconstructivism, a postmodernist style, is described as opposed to what?
o: The use of computer software in design
The expressive use of new materials
The ordered rationality of modern design
n: Deconstructivism opposes the ordered rationality of modern design. It relies on computer software rather than rejecting it.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Deconstructivism

q: From when is High-Tech Architecture dated in the movements table?
n: High-Tech runs from 1970 onwards, starting just as the International Style (1940–70) ends.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: High-Tech Architecture

q: What dates does the high-tech list give for the Pompidou Centre in Paris?
n: The Pompidou Centre is dated 1971–78. The range 1978–86 is Lloyd's of London, Rogers's next major high-tech building.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous High-Tech Buildings

q: Which materials replace traditional brickwork in high-tech architecture?
o: Steel, light metal panels, glass, and plastic derivatives
n: High-tech uses steel, light metal panels, glass, and plastics. Stained glass and ceramics belong to Art Nouveau interiors.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: High-Tech Architecture

q: Which firm designed the Allianz Arena in Munich (2005)?
n: Herzog & de Meuron designed the Allianz Arena, the latest building on the high-tech list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous High-Tech Buildings

q: The Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao (1991–97) was designed by whom?
n: Frank O. Gehry designed the Guggenheim Bilbao, one of four Gehry works across the deconstructivist and blob lists.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous Examples of Deconstructivism

q: Who curated the 1988 Deconstructivist Architecture exhibition?
n: Philip Johnson and Mark Wigley curated the show. Johnson also appears on these pages as a champion of the International Style, decades earlier.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Deconstructivism

q: High-tech architecture is rooted in which 19th-century avant-garde structures?
o: The Eiffel Tower and the Crystal Palace
The Home Insurance Building and the Marquette Building
The Houses of Parliament and Tower Bridge
The Paris Opera and the Louvre
n: The Eiffel Tower and the Crystal Palace are its roots, both made of exposed iron and glass. The Chicago buildings pioneered the steel frame but hid it behind masonry.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: High-Tech Architecture

q: Who designed the Channel Tunnel Waterloo Terminal in London (1993)?
n: Nicholas Grimshaw designed the Waterloo Terminal.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous High-Tech Buildings

q: Which of these deconstructivist buildings is NOT by Frank O. Gehry?
n: The Seattle Central Library (2004) is by Rem Koolhaas. The other three are Gehry's, in Los Angeles, Bilbao, and Prague.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous Examples of Deconstructivism

q: Which Frank O. Gehry building is in Los Angeles (1988–2003)?
n: The Walt Disney Concert Hall is Gehry's Los Angeles building. The Experience Music Project is in Seattle and is listed under blobitecture.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous Examples of Deconstructivism

q: Lloyd's of London (1978–86) is by which architect?
n: Richard Rogers designed Lloyd's of London on his own after the Pompidou partnership with Piano.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous High-Tech Buildings

q: The Kansai Airport Terminal in Osaka (1994) is the work of which architect?
n: Renzo Piano designed the Kansai Airport Terminal, his solo high-tech entry after the Pompidou Centre.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous High-Tech Buildings

q: Who designed the USA Pavilion at Expo 67 in Montreal?
n: Buckminster Fuller designed the USA Pavilion, the geodesic dome at the same Expo 67 that affirmed high-tech. Frei Otto is paired with Behnisch for Munich's Olympiapark.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous High-Tech Buildings

q: In high-tech architecture, what determines the new building shapes?
o: The shape of the components used
Computer software from the aerospace industry
n: High-tech drops traditional methods like brickwork, so the shape of the building follows the components it is made from. Aerospace-derived software is what enabled deconstructivist and blob shapes.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: High-Tech Architecture

q: Which exhibition affirmed the new high-tech approach?
o: The 1988 Deconstructivist Architecture show at MoMA
n: Expo 67 in Montreal is the exhibition named for high-tech. The 1988 MoMA show introduced Deconstructivism instead.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: High-Tech Architecture

q: Both the Multiplex Cinema (1993–8) and the UFA-Kristall Filmpalast (1998) in Dresden are by which designers?
n: Coop Himmelblau designed both Dresden cinemas. Peter Cook and Colin Fournier are listed for the Kunsthaus Graz under blobitecture.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous Examples of Deconstructivism

q: High-tech is symbolised by the Pompidou Centre in Paris. Which engineers worked with Renzo Piano and Richard Rogers on it?
n: Piano and Rogers designed the Pompidou Centre with engineers Ove Arup & Partners. Foster & Partners is an architecture firm, credited with the Hong Kong and Shanghai Bank.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: High-Tech Architecture

q: What made the unusual shapes of deconstructivist buildings possible?
o: Cheap steel after World War II
Tubular structural systems from Fazlur Khan
Design software developed from the aerospace industry
n: Aerospace-derived design software made the distorted shapes buildable. Fazlur Khan's tube systems solved a different problem, the height of supertall towers.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Deconstructivism

q: Daniel Libeskind's deconstructivist works in the list are in which two cities?
n: Libeskind designed the Imperial War Museum North in Manchester (2002) and the Royal Ontario Museum extension in Toronto (2007). Dresden is Coop Himmelblau's city on the list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous Examples of Deconstructivism

q: Which deconstructivist building by Frank O. Gehry is in Prague (1992–97)?
n: The Nationale Nederlanden Building is Gehry's Prague work. The Imperial War Museum North and the Royal Ontario Museum extension are both Libeskind's.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous Examples of Deconstructivism

q: Who is described as probably the most famous deconstructivist designer in America?
n: Frank O. Gehry (b. 1929) is named as America's best-known deconstructivist. Libeskind is named as one of the leading figures in Europe.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Deconstructivism

q: Coop Himmelblau was founded by which three architects?
o: Günter Behnisch, Frei Otto, and Buckminster Fuller
Jacques Herzog, Pierre de Meuron, and Rem Koolhaas
Lars Spuybroek, Kas Oosterhuis, and Peter Cook
Wolf Prix, Helmut Swiczinsky, and Michael Holzer
n: Wolf Prix, Helmut Swiczinsky, and Michael Holzer founded Coop Himmelblau. Spuybroek and Oosterhuis are the blobitecture designers of the Water Pavilion.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Deconstructivism

q: What is high-tech architecture fundamentally based on?
o: The distortion of geometry through non-rectilinear shapes
The revival of historical orders and proportions
Openly expressing the newest technology and materials
n: High-tech expresses the latest technology and materials openly. Distorted non-rectilinear geometry is the mark of Deconstructivism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: High-Tech Architecture

q: In Europe, the top deconstructivists are said to be Daniel Libeskind and which firm?
n: Libeskind (b. 1946) and Coop Himmelblau are the leading European names. Herzog & de Meuron appear under high-tech for the Allianz Arena.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Deconstructivism

q: Art Deco and Art Nouveau both embraced every kind of art. How did Art Deco differ from its predecessor?
o: It was ornament for its own sake, without theory or politics behind it
It carried a strong political programme
n: Art Deco was purely decorative and had no theory or politics behind it. That is the table's point of contrast with Art Nouveau.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Art Deco Architecture

q: The International Style was championed by Philip Johnson and by the Second Chicago School, led by whom?
n: The ex-Bauhaus émigré Mies van der Rohe led the Second Chicago School. Sullivan belongs to the first Chicago School of the 1880s.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: International Style of Modern Architecture

q: What date range does the movements table give for Totalitarian Architecture?
n: Totalitarian Architecture runs from 1933 to 1960, from Hitler's rise to Mao's Great Hall of the People in 1959.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Totalitarian Architecture

q: The Inland Steel Building in Chicago (1957) is credited to which firm?
n: Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed the Inland Steel Building. The other three are first Chicago School firms from the 1880s–1900s.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous International Style Buildings

q: Which description fits totalitarian buildings?
o: Human-scaled, asymmetrical, and free of ornament
Gargantuan, often with Greek elements, embodying the leader's megalomania
Light steel frames with exposed services
Organic, bulging shapes produced by software
n: Totalitarian buildings were built at gargantuan scale, often borrowed from Greek architecture, and expressed the fantasies and megalomania of the leader.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Totalitarian Architecture

q: The New Reich Chancellery in Berlin (1938–9) was designed by whom?
n: Albert Speer, Hitler's architect, designed the New Reich Chancellery. He also appears among revivalists for the German Pavilion in Paris.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Examples of Totalitarian Architectural Design

q: The entrance foyer of the Strand Palace Hotel (1930) is an Art Deco work by whom?
n: The table credits the Strand Palace Hotel foyer to Oliver Bernhard. Charles Holden's London building on these pages is the "Ziggurat" 55 Broadway.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Art Deco Buildings

q: What date range does the movements table give for the International Style of Modern Architecture?
n: The International Style is dated 1940–70. High-Tech picks up from 1970 onwards.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: International Style of Modern Architecture

q: Which building by Zhang Bo (1959) is listed as totalitarian architecture?
o: Great Hall of the People, Beijing
Bank of China Tower, Hong Kong
n: Zhang Bo designed the Great Hall of the People in Beijing. The Bank of China Tower is a 1990 supertall by I.M. Pei's firm, not a Mao-era building.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Examples of Totalitarian Architectural Design

q: The Art Deco list credits the Entrance Plaza to Rockefeller Center (1932–9) to whom?
n: The Entrance Plaza is credited to various designers. The Rockefeller Center complex itself appears on the skyscraper list under Hofmeister, Hood, Godley, and Fouilhoux.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Art Deco Buildings

q: What date range does the movements table give for Art Deco Architecture?
n: The movements table dates Art Deco architecture 1925–1940. The style timeline on page 1 stops it at 1937, so the two tables differ by three years.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Art Deco Architecture

q: The Seagram Building in New York (1954–58) was designed by which pair?
o: Mies van der Rohe and Philip Johnson
n: Mies van der Rohe and Philip Johnson designed the Seagram Building, uniting the two champions of the International Style named in the description.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous International Style Buildings

q: Which of these New York buildings is NOT on the Art Deco buildings list?
n: The Chanin, Empire State, and Chrysler buildings all appear under Art Deco. The Woolworth Building (1913) is listed only as a New York skyscraper, and it predates Art Deco.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, pp. 3–4 — Art Deco Buildings

q: Moscow State University (1953) was designed by which architect?
n: Lev Vladimirovich Rudnev designed Moscow State University, the Stalin-era example. Zhang Bo is the Chinese architect of the Great Hall of the People.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Examples of Totalitarian Architectural Design

q: Several architects tried to apply the International Style to residential buildings. Which is NOT named among them?
n: Neutra, Lescaze, and Stone are the names tied to residential use. Philip Johnson appears as a champion of the style, not as one of the residential designers.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: International Style of Modern Architecture

q: Who designed the Olympic Stadium in Berlin (1934–6)?
n: Werner March designed the 1936 Berlin Olympic Stadium. Albert Speer's Berlin entry is the New Reich Chancellery, and Behnisch built the later Munich Olympiapark.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Examples of Totalitarian Architectural Design

q: Emery Roth designed which Art Deco building in New York (1931)?
n: Emery Roth (1871–1948) designed the El Dorado Apartment Building.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Art Deco Buildings

q: The International Style entered American architecture in the 1930s. When did it become the dominant fashion?
o: During the major post-war urban development phase, 1955–1970
n: It became dominant during the post-war urban development boom of 1955–1970, when corporate towers went up across American cities.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: International Style of Modern Architecture

q: Art Deco architecture was also inspired by the ziggurat designs of which ancient art?
n: The stepped ziggurat comes from Mesopotamian art, and it shows up in Art Deco setbacks. Egyptian art is also an Art Deco source, but for motifs rather than ziggurats.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Art Deco Architecture

q: Who designed the Lake Shore Drive Apartments in Chicago (1948–51)?
n: The Lake Shore Drive Apartments are by Mies van der Rohe. SOM's Chicago entry is the Inland Steel Building.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous International Style Buildings

q: Walter Gropius's International Style work in the list is The Graduate Center at which university (1950)?
n: Gropius designed The Graduate Center at Harvard, where he taught after leaving Germany.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous International Style Buildings

q: Totalitarian architecture was produced under which dictators, according to the table?
o: Kaiser Wilhelm II, Tsar Nicholas II, and Emperor Meiji
Napoleon, Louis XIV, and Peter the Great
Adolf Hitler, Joseph Stalin, and Chairman Mao
n: The table names Hitler, Stalin, and Mao, whose buildings are the Berlin, Moscow, and Beijing examples in the list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Totalitarian Architecture

q: Which Art Deco building in New York (1929–30) is credited to Raymond Hood?
n: Raymond Hood designed the McGraw-Hill Building. The El Dorado is by Emery Roth and the Chanin by Sloan and Robertson.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Art Deco Buildings

q: The International Style was used mainly for which building type?
n: It was mainly used for corporate office blocks, despite some architects' efforts to bring it to houses.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: International Style of Modern Architecture

q: In which countries did the International Style first appear during the 1920s?
n: The style began in Germany, Holland, and France, then crossed to the United States in the 1930s.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: International Style of Modern Architecture

q: What was totalitarian architecture designed to do?
o: Awe the regime's subjects and impress foreign visitors
Show off the latest structural technology
n: These buildings were meant to awe citizens and impress foreigners. Minimal-cost housing is the aim of Social Housing architecture.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Totalitarian Architecture

q: Which combination of sources influenced Art Deco?
o: Concrete art, Cubism, and left-wing politics
The geometrics of Cubism, the movement of Futurism, and Pre-Columbian and Egyptian art
Arts & Crafts ideals and abstract floral motifs
Constructivism, De Stijl, and Frank Lloyd Wright
n: Art Deco mixed Cubist geometry, Futurist movement, and ancient Pre-Columbian and Egyptian art. Concrete art, Cubism, and left-wing politics is the De Stijl list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: Art Deco Architecture

q: Why was the International Style considered ideal for skyscrapers?
o: Its sleek modern look and its use of steel and glass
Its massive stone walls and small windows
Its revival of the stepped ziggurat
n: The sleek modern look and steel-and-glass construction suited tall office towers. The stepped ziggurat is an Art Deco source.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Movements: International Style of Modern Architecture

q: The fourth-tallest 20th-century tower on the list (1974), now destroyed, stood 417 m / 1,368 ft. Which was it?
n: One World Trade Center in New York (1974) is listed as destroyed, at 417 m. It is the only tower on the list that no longer stands.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Tallest Towers Built in the 20th Century

q: The Water Pavilion (1993–1997) was designed by which pair?
n: Lars Spuybroek and Kas Oosterhuis designed the Water Pavilion, the earliest blob example listed. Cook and Fournier did the Kunsthaus Graz.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous Examples of Blobitecture

q: Who christened the term 'blobitecture', and where?
o: William Safire, in the New York Times in 2002
Philip Johnson, in a MoMA catalogue
Charles Jencks, in a book on postmodernism
n: William Safire coined 'blobitecture' in the New York Times in 2002. Greg Lynn's contribution was the earlier phrase 'blob architecture' (1995).
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Blobitecture

q: The Kunsthaus in Graz (2003) was designed by whom?
n: Peter Cook and Colin Fournier designed the Kunsthaus Graz. Coop Himmelblau is Austrian too, but its listed works are the Dresden cinemas.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous Examples of Blobitecture

q: Blobitecture was developed by whom, according to the table?
o: Postmodernist artists on both sides of the Atlantic
Engineers of the aerospace industry alone
Former Bauhaus teachers in the United States
n: The table credits postmodernist artists in Europe and America. The aerospace industry supplied the software, not the style.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Blobitecture

q: The style itself first appeared in the early 1990s. In what year did architect Greg Lynn use the term 'blob architecture'?
n: Greg Lynn used 'blob architecture' in 1995, seven years before Safire's 2002 coinage of 'blobitecture'.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Blobitecture

q: What did the new tubular structural designs achieve for skyscrapers?
o: They allowed buildings to be clad in stone again
They removed the need for elevators above 50 storeys
They cut the steel needed and freed architects from box-like design
They made emergency evacuation procedures unnecessary
n: Tube structures used much less steel and let towers break away from the regular box. Evacuation, far from being solved, is named as the main remaining limit.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Late 20th-Century Supertall Towers

q: The Sage Gateshead (2004) and the Philological Library at the Free University, Berlin (2005) share which architect?
n: Both are by Norman Foster, who appears under high-tech too through Foster & Partners' Hong Kong and Shanghai Bank.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous Examples of Blobitecture

q: Jin Mao Tower in Shanghai (1999), at 421 m / 1,380 ft, holds which rank on the list?
n: Jin Mao Tower ranks third, behind Petronas Towers (452 m) and Willis Tower (442 m).
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Tallest Towers Built in the 20th Century

q: The Empire State Building (1931) appears on the tallest-towers list at what rank and height?
n: The Empire State Building ranks seventh at 381 m / 1,250 ft, the oldest tower on the list by four decades.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Tallest Towers Built in the 20th Century

q: Which tower is ranked second, at 442 m / 1,450 ft (1973)?
n: Willis Tower in Chicago (1973) is second at 442 m. One World Trade Center, finished a year later, is fourth at 417 m.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Tallest Towers Built in the 20th Century

q: CITIC Plaza, ranked fifth at 391 m / 1,283 ft (1997), is in which city?
n: CITIC Plaza is in Guangzhou. Shenzhen is home to Shun Hing Square, ranked sixth.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Tallest Towers Built in the 20th Century

q: Frank O. Gehry appears on the blobitecture list for which Seattle building (1999–2000)?
n: Gehry's Experience Music Project in Seattle is listed as blobitecture. The Seattle Central Library is Rem Koolhaas's deconstructivist work in the same city.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous Examples of Blobitecture

q: How tall does the table list the Petronas Towers in Kuala Lumpur?
n: Petronas Towers: 452 m, or 1,483 ft. 442 m is Willis Tower and 421 m is Jin Mao Tower.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Tallest Towers Built in the 20th Century

q: Which tower tops the list of the tallest towers built in the 20th century?
n: The Petronas Towers (1998) rank first at 452 m. Willis Tower is second at 442 m.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Tallest Towers Built in the 20th Century

q: The structural techniques behind a new generation of supertall towers were developed by US architects such as Fazlur Khan of which firm?
n: Fazlur Khan (1929–82) worked at Skidmore, Owings & Merrill. Shreve, Lamb & Harmon built the Empire State Building with an older steel frame.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Late 20th-Century Supertall Towers

q: Which tower is in Shenzhen, ranked sixth at 384 m / 1,260 ft (1996)?
n: Shun Hing Square is the Shenzhen tower. Central Plaza is in Hong Kong and Tuntex Sky Tower in Kaohsiung.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Tallest Towers Built in the 20th Century

q: Tuntex Sky Tower (1997), ranked eighth at 378 m / 1,240 ft, is located where?
n: Tuntex Sky Tower is in Kaohsiung, Taiwan. Taipei is the tempting guess, but it is not on this list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Tallest Towers Built in the 20th Century

q: The Bus Station at Spaarne Hospital (2003) is credited to which firm?
n: NIO Architecten designed the Spaarne Hospital bus station.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Famous Examples of Blobitecture

q: Which tower closes the top-ten list, at 367 m / 1,205 ft (1990)?
o: Bank of China Tower, Hong Kong
n: The Bank of China Tower in Hong Kong is tenth at 367 m. Central Plaza, also in Hong Kong, is ninth at 374 m.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Tallest Towers Built in the 20th Century

q: A 1990s postmodernist style is known for organic, rounded, bulging shapes. What is it called?
n: Blobitecture is the style of bulging, rounded forms, dated to the 1990s. Deconstructivism is its cousin, but it distorts geometry with angular, non-rectilinear shapes.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Blobitecture

q: Blobitecture is also known by which other names?
n: The table gives blobism and blobismus as alternative names.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Blobitecture

q: Which Hong Kong tower is ranked ninth, at 374 m / 1,227 ft (1992)?
n: Central Plaza is ninth. The other Hong Kong tower on the list, Bank of China Tower, is tenth at 367 m.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Tallest Towers Built in the 20th Century

q: The construction of blobitecture's non-geometric structures depends heavily on which software?
n: Blob buildings rely on CATIA, which the table spells "CATID". It is aerospace design software, the same kind of tool that enabled deconstructivist shapes.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Blobitecture

q: With towers now regularly exceeding 100 storeys, what does the table name as the biggest limitation on upward growth?
o: Safety and the lack of emergency evacuation procedures
Wind sway at the top floors
n: The biggest limit is safety, specifically the lack of emergency evacuation procedures. Steel cost was the 19th-century issue that the tube designs later reduced.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 5 — Movements: Late 20th-Century Supertall Towers

q: The Chicago Stock Exchange (1893–94) and the Prudential (Guaranty) Building in Buffalo (1894) were designed by which partnership?
n: Both are by Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan. The Guaranty Building in Buffalo is the one outside Chicago, which is why it is often misattributed to Burnham.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Chicago School of Architecture

q: In which building was a metal skeleton frame first used?
n: Jenney's Home Insurance Building of 1884 is named as the first use of a metal skeleton frame. The other three are later Chicago School buildings by Holabird & Roche, Adler & Sullivan, and Burnham.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Chicago School of Architecture

q: Which architect designed the "Roman" Milan Train Station (1931)?
n: Ulisse Stacchini designed Milan's station. Piacentini is the other Italian on the list, credited with City University, Rome.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: The Flatiron Building in New York and the Heyworth Building in Chicago came from which firm?
n: Daniel Burnham's firm designed the Flatiron (1901–3) and the Heyworth Building (1904), as well as the Fisher Building. It shows a Chicago firm working in New York.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Chicago School of Architecture

q: Hotel Tassel (1892–3) and the Maison du Peuple (1896–9) in Brussels are the work of which architect?
n: Victor Horta (1861–1947) designed both Brussels buildings. Guimard is the French counterpart, remembered for the Paris Metro entrances.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Art Nouveau Architecture

q: The Marquette Building (1895) and the Gage Group Buildings on S. Michigan Avenue (1899) were designed by which firm?
n: Both are by William Holabird and Martin Roche, who also did the Chicago Building (1904–5) and Brooks Building (1909–10). McKim, Mead & White were East Coast classicists, not Chicago School.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Chicago School of Architecture

q: Villa Ruggeri in Pesaro (1902), a Stile Liberty work, was designed by whom?
n: Giuseppe Brega (1877–1960) is the Stile Liberty architect of Villa Ruggeri. Stacchini and Piacentini are also Italian, but they appear under Revivalist and Totalitarian works.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Art Nouveau Architecture

q: Who designed the "Classical" Lincoln Memorial in Washington DC (1922)?
n: Henry Bacon designed the Lincoln Memorial. Cass Gilbert is the Woolworth Building's architect, another American who worked in historical dress.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: Which building by Charles Holden (1929) is tagged as a "Ziggurat" revival?
n: Charles Holden's 55 Broadway in London carries the "Ziggurat" tag, echoing stepped Mesopotamian forms.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: Who founded the Vienna Secession and designed its headquarters?
n: Joseph Maria Olbrich (1867–1908) founded the Vienna Secession and designed its building. Loos also worked in Vienna, but he is listed as an Early Modernist and was a critic of ornament.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Art Nouveau Architecture

q: What date range does the movements table give for the Chicago School of Architecture?
n: The Chicago School is dated 1880–1910. The range 1900–30 belongs to its successor in high-rise building, the New York School of Skyscraper Architecture.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Chicago School of Architecture

q: The table lists Gaudí's Sagrada Família (1883–1926) as a revival of which style?
n: Sagrada Família is tagged as a "Gothic" revival building. Gaudí also appears under Art Nouveau for Casa Milà, so he shows up in two movements.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: The use of steel and iron was first highlighted by a French architect and then used by Louis Sullivan and others. Who was that French architect?
n: Viollet-le-Duc first highlighted steel and iron, and Sullivan took the idea up in Chicago. Guimard was also French, but he is listed for Art Nouveau Metro entrances.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Chicago School of Architecture

q: What date range does the movements table give for Revivalist Architecture?
n: Revivalist Architecture spans 1900–2000, the widest range in the table, because its examples run from Sagrada Família to the 1998 Louvre Pyramid.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: The Viceroy's Palace in India (1930), tagged "Classical"/"Mughal", was designed by whom?
n: Edwin Lutyens designed the Viceroy's Palace, mixing classical and Mughal elements, which explains the double tag.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: Stockholm City Hall (1923), tagged as "Medieval" revival, was designed by whom?
n: Ragnar Östberg designed Stockholm City Hall. Eliel Saarinen is the other Nordic name nearby, but his Helsinki Train Station is listed as Early Modernist.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: Why is the 'Chicago School' not a school in the usual sense?
o: It was a city office that approved all tall buildings
It was a university department that trained engineers
It was a manifesto group bound by one written creed
It was a centre of high-rise building with no unified set of principles
n: The table calls it a centre of high-rise development rather than a school as such. Its members shared no unified principles, so their designs, techniques, and materials varied.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Chicago School of Architecture

q: What date range does the movements table give for Art Nouveau architecture?
n: The movements table dates Art Nouveau architecture 1890–1920. The style timeline on page 1 ends it earlier, at 1914, so check which table a question is drawn from.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Art Nouveau Architecture

q: City University in Rome (1935) appears under both Revivalist and Totalitarian architecture. Who designed it?
n: Marcello Piacentini designed City University, Rome. It is tagged "Classical" among revivalist buildings and also listed as an example of totalitarian design under Mussolini.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, pp. 2 and 4 — Revivalist and Totalitarian Architecture

q: Who is credited with founding the Chicago School of Architecture?
n: William Le Baron Jenney (1832–1907) founded the school with other innovative American architects. Sullivan is the most famous member, which makes him the usual wrong guess.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Chicago School of Architecture

q: The AEG Turbine Factory in Berlin (1909), tagged as a "Classical" revival building, was by which architect?
n: Peter Behrens built the AEG Turbine Factory, and the table lists it under both Revivalist and Early Modernist architecture. Gropius worked for Behrens but his own early factory is the Fagus Factory.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: In which century did revivalism reach its peak, with Romanesque, Gothic, and Beaux-Arts structures in Europe and the United States?
n: Revivalism reached its apogee in 19th-century architecture, then carried on into the 20th century. That continuation is why the movement is still dated 1900–2000.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: Which Chicago School architect pioneered new foundation techniques?
n: Dankmar Adler is credited with the new foundation techniques. He was the engineering half of Adler & Sullivan, while Sullivan led the design.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Chicago School of Architecture

q: Which architect designed Hearst Castle at San Simeon (1939), tagged "Greek"/"Moorish"?
n: Julia Morgan designed Hearst Castle, the only woman in the revivalist list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: Which of these buildings is NOT by Holabird & Roche?
n: The Fisher Building (1895–6) is by Burnham and Co. Holabird & Roche's list is the Marquette, Gage Group, Chicago, and Brooks buildings.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Chicago School of Architecture

q: The "Classical" German Pavilion at the Paris World Exhibition (1937) was designed by whom?
n: Albert Speer designed the German Pavilion. Speer also appears under Totalitarian Architecture for the New Reich Chancellery, while Werner March built the Berlin Olympic Stadium.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: Which Art Nouveau architect is famous for his entrances to the Paris Metro?
n: Hector Guimard (1867–1942) designed the Paris Metro entrances. Horta worked in Brussels, not Paris.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Art Nouveau Architecture

q: Designers have turned to the past for inspiration ever since which group revived the proportions and orders of Roman architecture?
n: The table traces revivalism back to the Italian Renaissance, when architects brought back Roman proportions and orders. Beaux-Arts is one of the later revivals, not the starting point.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: Which Art Nouveau architect designed Casa Milà (La Pedrera) in Barcelona (1906–10)?
n: Casa Milà is by Antoni Gaudí (1852–1926). Horta is the Brussels Art Nouveau architect, known for Hotel Tassel.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Art Nouveau Architecture

q: Henry Hobson Richardson (1838–86) is listed as a designer in which revival style?
n: Richardson is the Neo-Romanesque designer, the source of the term 'Richardsonian Romanesque'. Neo-Gothic belongs to James Renwick.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: A decorative style of flowing lines and abstract floral motifs was closely associated with which earlier movement?
o: The Arts and Crafts movement of William Morris
n: Art Nouveau is tied to the Arts and Crafts movement championed by William Morris (1834–96). The Werkbund and Bauhaus came later and pushed toward industry and plain forms.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Art Nouveau Architecture

q: I.M. Pei's Louvre Pyramid (1998) is tagged as a revival of which tradition?
n: The pyramid form is tagged "Egyptian". "Ziggurat" is the tag for Holden's 55 Broadway, the other ancient Near Eastern reference.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: The Glasgow School of Art (1907) was designed by which Art Nouveau architect?
n: Charles Rennie Mackintosh (1868–1928) designed the Glasgow School of Art, the Scottish landmark of the style.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Art Nouveau Architecture

q: In Germany, Art Nouveau was known by what name?
n: Jugendstil is the German name. Stile Liberty is the Italian term, as used for Brega's Villa Ruggeri, and the Secession was the Vienna group Olbrich founded.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Art Nouveau Architecture

q: James Renwick (1818–95) is listed as what kind of revivalist?
n: Renwick is the Neo-Gothic architect. Neo-Romanesque is the label for Henry Hobson Richardson, listed right below him.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: Paul Bonatz's Stuttgart Train Station (1928) is tagged as a revival of which style?
n: Stuttgart Train Station is labelled "Romanesque". "Roman" is the tag on a different station, Stacchini's Milan Train Station.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: Art Nouveau interiors were lavishly decorated with which kinds of applied art?
n: The style covered both exterior and interior, and interiors carried applied art such as stained glass and ceramics. Exposed services belong to high-tech, and raw concrete to brutalism.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Art Nouveau Architecture

q: In the revivalism description, which period bracket is attached to the Romanesque buildings that were revived?
n: The movements table gives Romanesque as 1000–1150 and Gothic as 1150–1300. The style timeline on page 1 uses broader ranges (800–1200 and 1100–1450), so the two tables do not match.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: Which firm designed the "Classical" Pennsylvania Railway Station (1910)?
n: Pennsylvania Railway Station is by McKim, Mead & White. Shreve, Lamb & Harmon built the Empire State Building, and SOM belongs to the International Style and supertall towers.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 2 — Movements: Revivalist Architecture

q: Le Corbusier was born with what name?
n: Le Corbusier (1887–1965) was born Charles-Edouard Jeanneret. Pierre Jeanneret was his cousin and collaborator, which is what makes that option tempting.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Early Modernist Architects

q: Which firm appears in both the Chicago School list and the New York skyscraper list, thanks to the Flatiron Building?
n: Burnham's firm designed the Flatiron Building in New York, so it bridges the Chicago School and the New York School. The other three appear only on the New York list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, pp. 2–3 — Chicago School and Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: Which quality was a key aspect of the modernist style?
n: Functionality was central to modernism. Monumentality fits Totalitarian architecture, and ornament is what modernists removed.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: Early Modernist Architecture

q: What condition in New York and Chicago made steel-frame high-rises attractive in the first place?
o: Rapid development with limited available space
Abundant cheap land on the city edge
n: Both cities were developing rapidly but had little space to spread into, so the only way to add floor area was to build up.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: New York School of Skyscraper Architecture

q: Villa Savoye (1931) and the Unité d'Habitation in Marseille (1952) are works of which architect?
n: Both are by Le Corbusier. Mies van der Rohe is the other great modernist of that generation, but his listed works include the Seagram Building and Lake Shore Drive Apartments.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Early Modernist Architects

q: Which architect designed Helsinki Train Station (1904–14)?
n: Eliel Saarinen (1873–1950) designed Helsinki Train Station. Ragnar Östberg's Nordic landmark is Stockholm City Hall.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Early Modernist Architects

q: The Lincoln Building in New York (1930) was designed by which firm?
n: The Lincoln Building is by J.E. Carpenter & Associates.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: Peter Behrens's AEG Turbine Factory (1909) is listed under Revivalist Architecture and under which other movement?
n: Behrens is one of the Famous Early Modernist Architects for the AEG Turbine Factory, even though the revivalist list tags the same building "Classical".
ref: History of Architecture Tables, pp. 2–3 — Revivalist and Early Modernist Architecture

q: The Empire State Building was designed by which firm?
n: Shreve, Lamb & Harmon designed the Empire State Building. It is listed among the New York skyscrapers, the Art Deco buildings, and the tallest 20th-century towers.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: Rockefeller Center in New York (1940) is credited to which team?
n: Rockefeller Center is credited to Hofmeister, Hood, Godley, and Fouilhoux. Its entrance plaza is listed separately under Art Deco as the work of various designers.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: Ernest Flagg designed which New York skyscraper (1908)?
n: The Singer Building is Ernest Flagg's. The Metropolitan Tower, finished a year later, is by Napoleon Le Brun & Sons.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: What date range does the movements table give for Early Modernist Architecture?
n: Early Modernist Architecture is dated 1900–30, the same span as the New York School. Expressionism (1910–25) sits inside that range as a reaction to it.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: Early Modernist Architecture

q: Between 1900 and 1930, one city led the world in advanced skyscraper design. Which city was it?
n: New York took the lead from 1900 to 1930. Chicago had pioneered the steel frame earlier, which is why it is the tempting wrong answer.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: New York School of Skyscraper Architecture

q: The modernist format was later fully realised in the United States. Which example does the table give?
o: The AEG Turbine Factory in Berlin
The Larkin Administration Building in Buffalo
Henry Ford's assembly plant at Rouge River, south of Detroit
n: Henry Ford's Rouge River plant, then the largest manufacturing plant in the world, is the US example. The Fagus and AEG factories are European early modernist works.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: Early Modernist Architecture

q: Walter Gropius's early modernist Fagus Factory (1911) is located where?
n: The Fagus Factory is at Alfeld-an-der-Leine. Dessau is where Gropius later built the Bauhaus Complex (1925).
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Early Modernist Architects

q: Robie House in Chicago (1910) and Fallingwater at Bear Run, PA (1937) are by which early modernist?
n: Both houses are by Frank Lloyd Wright (1867–1959). Loos also designed houses in this period, but his are Steiner House and Moller House in Vienna.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Early Modernist Architects

q: Which partnership designed the Daily News Building in New York (1929)?
n: The Daily News Building is by Howells & Hood. Raymond Hood also appears alone for the McGraw-Hill Building and in the Rockefeller Center team.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: Which architect designed the Chrysler Building?
n: The Chrysler Building is by William Van Alen, and it is listed as both a New York skyscraper and an Art Deco building.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: Philadelphia City Hall (1908), included among the famous early skyscrapers, was designed by whom?
o: John McArthur and Thomas U. Walter
n: John McArthur and Thomas U. Walter are credited with Philadelphia City Hall. It is the one building on the list outside New York.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: Which architect designed the Woolworth Building in New York (1913)?
n: Cass Gilbert designed the Woolworth Building. William Van Alen is the Chrysler Building's architect.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: Which economic change suddenly made building upward much more attractive?
o: A fall in the price of steel
The arrival of cheap reinforced concrete
A rise in property taxes on low buildings
n: The table ties the high-rise boom to cheaper steel, the main material for tall frames. Concrete and zoning are not the reason it gives.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: New York School of Skyscraper Architecture

q: In the 19th century, American architects pioneered steel-frame high-rise building in which two cities?
n: New York and Chicago are the two cities named. Both were growing fast while their usable space stayed limited, which pushed buildings upward.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: New York School of Skyscraper Architecture

q: Steiner House (1910) and Moller House (1928) in Vienna were designed by whom?
n: Both houses are by Adolf Loos (1870–1933). Olbrich is also Viennese, but he is listed for the Secession building under Art Nouveau.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Early Modernist Architects

q: What date range does the movements table give for the New York School of Skyscraper Architecture?
n: The New York School is dated 1900–30, the three decades in which New York led in tall buildings. The range 1880–1910 is the Chicago School that came before it.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: New York School of Skyscraper Architecture

q: Craig Severance designed which New York skyscraper (1930)?
n: Craig Severance designed the Bank of Manhattan Trust Building. Its rival for height that same year was William Van Alen's Chrysler Building.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: Who designed the Metropolitan Tower in New York (1909)?
n: The Metropolitan Tower is by Napoleon Le Brun & Sons. J.E. Carpenter & Associates appear for the Lincoln Building of 1930.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: How did early modernist buildings treat history and materials?
o: They applied rich ornament over steel frames
They revived Roman proportions in dressed stone
They used rough brick and timber to recall local crafts
They largely avoided historical associations and used iron, steel, glass, and concrete
n: Early modernism was relatively, if not wholly, free of historical associations and made full use of the newest techniques and materials. Reviving Roman proportions is the revivalist approach.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: Early Modernist Architecture

q: Modernist architecture, called the first real architecture of the 20th century, was designed for whom?
n: Modernist architecture was designed for "modern man". Building for the state and its leaders is what defines Totalitarian architecture.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: Early Modernist Architecture

q: Who designed the Chanin Building in New York?
n: The Chanin Building is by Sloan & Robertson. It is also listed as an Art Deco building.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: Who designed the Park Row Building in New York (1899–1901)?
n: Robert Henderson Robertson designed the Park Row Building, the earliest on the New York list. Ernest Flagg's entry is the Singer Building.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous New York Skyscrapers

q: Which abstract painter was an active member of De Stijl?
n: Piet Mondrian (1872–1944) was an active De Stijl member, alongside architects, designers, and sculptors. Kandinsky and Klee taught at the Bauhaus instead.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: De Stijl Avant-Garde Architecture

q: A 1920s building has curves, spirals, and non-symmetrical elements, and plays up the expressive value of its materials. Which movement does it fit?
n: Curves, spirals, asymmetry, and expressive materials are the Expressionist traits. De Stijl is the opposite: right angles and primary colours.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: Expressionist Architecture

q: Max Berg designed which expressionist building (1913)?
n: Max Berg (1870–1947) designed the Centenary Hall in Breslau. The Scheepvaarthuis was co-designed by Michel de Klerk.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Expressionist Architects

q: The Chilehaus in Hamburg (1921–4) was designed by whom?
n: Johannes Friedrich (Fritz) Höger designed the Chilehaus, the Hamburg entry on the expressionist list.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Expressionist Architects

q: What date range does the movements table give for De Stijl Avant-Garde Architecture?
n: De Stijl runs from 1917, the year the group was founded, to 1930. The range 1919–1933 is the Bauhaus.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: De Stijl Avant-Garde Architecture

q: In which Dutch city was the De Stijl group founded?
n: De Stijl was founded in Leiden in 1917. Utrecht is where Rietveld built the Schröder House, and Rotterdam is where Oud was housing architect.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: De Stijl Avant-Garde Architecture

q: Which influences shaped De Stijl?
o: Concrete art, Cubism, and radical left-wing politics
The Arts and Crafts movement and floral motifs
n: De Stijl drew on Concrete art and Cubism and on radical left-wing politics. Futurism, Pre-Columbian art, and ziggurats are Art Deco sources.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: De Stijl Avant-Garde Architecture

q: Bruno Taut's Glass Pavilion (1914) was built for which event?
o: The Weissenhof Estate Exhibition in Stuttgart
n: The Glass Pavilion stood at the 1914 Werkbund Exposition in Cologne. The Weissenhof Estate Exhibition was the 1927 modernist housing show.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Expressionist Architects

q: What was De Stijl's main objective?
o: The revival of medieval building crafts
A new generation of steel skyscrapers
A compositional method that works for both fine and decorative art
n: De Stijl wanted one compositional method for fine and decorative art alike, which is why a painting, a chair, and a house can look related. Minimal-cost housing is the goal of Social Housing architecture.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: De Stijl Avant-Garde Architecture

q: Which De Stijl architect was preoccupied with Communist politics and designs for prefabricated mass housing, worked out with P.J.C. Klaarhamer?
n: Robert van't Hoff (1887–1979) spent his De Stijl period on Communist politics and prefabricated housing with the Utrecht architect Klaarhamer.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous De Stijl Architects

q: Who founded the De Stijl group in 1917?
n: Theo van Doesburg (1883–1931) founded De Stijl. Mondrian is the group's most famous member, which makes him the classic wrong answer.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: De Stijl Avant-Garde Architecture

q: Rudolf Steiner is famous for which expressionist building (1914)?
n: Rudolf Steiner (1861–1925) built the Goetheanum at Dornach. The Einstein Tower is Erich Mendelsohn's.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Expressionist Architects

q: A design uses austere geometric shapes, right angles, and primary colours. Which movement is it?
n: Austere geometry, right angles, and primary colours define De Stijl. Expressionism is the contrast, with curves and asymmetry.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: De Stijl Avant-Garde Architecture

q: The Schröder House in Utrecht (1924), now a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and the Red and Blue Chair (1917) are by whom?
n: Gerrit Rietveld (1888–1964) designed both, and the house is named after him and his client, Rietveld Schröder House.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, pp. 3–4 — Famous De Stijl Architects

q: Expressionist architecture emerged in which region?
n: Expressionism came out of Germany and the Low Countries, which is why the listed works are in Berlin, Hamburg, Potsdam, and Amsterdam.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: Expressionist Architecture

q: Who designed the Grosses Schauspielhaus in Berlin (1919)?
n: Hans Poelzig (1869–1936) designed the Grosses Schauspielhaus. Bruno Taut's expressionist work is the Glass Pavilion in Cologne.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Expressionist Architects

q: Which building is cited as a contemporary example of expressionist architecture?
o: Guggenheim Museum, Bilbao by Frank Gehry
Sydney Opera House by Jørn Utzon
Pompidou Centre by Piano and Rogers
n: The Sydney Opera House (1973) by Jørn Utzon is the contemporary expressionist example. The Guggenheim Bilbao is listed under Deconstructivism instead.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: Expressionist Architecture

q: What date range does the movements table give for Expressionist Architecture?
n: Expressionist Architecture is dated 1910–25. De Stijl starts in 1917 and Social Housing in 1918, so all three overlap.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: Expressionist Architecture

q: Which expressionist architect co-designed the Scheepvaarthuis in Amsterdam (1918)?
n: Michel de Klerk (1884–1923) co-designed the Scheepvaarthuis. Oud and Rietveld are Dutch too, but they belong to De Stijl, the opposite camp.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Expressionist Architects

q: Which De Stijl architect served as Municipal Housing Architect for Rotterdam and took a key part in the Weissenhof Estate Exhibition (1927)?
n: J.J.P. Oud (1890–1963) was Rotterdam's housing architect and a key Weissenhof participant. Ernst May did similar work in Frankfurt, but he is not listed with De Stijl.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 4 — Famous De Stijl Architects

q: Erich Mendelsohn designed which building in Potsdam (1924)?
n: The Einstein Tower in Potsdam is Erich Mendelsohn's (1887–1953). The Goetheanum is Rudolf Steiner's building in Dornach.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Famous Expressionist Architects

q: Expressionist architects rebelled against what?
o: The floral ornament of Art Nouveau
The functionalist, industrial-style structures of modernism
The gargantuan scale of totalitarian buildings
n: Expressionists turned against modernism's functionalist industrial structures and preferred sinuous or highly articulated forms. Totalitarian architecture came later, from 1933.
ref: History of Architecture Tables, p. 3 — Movements: Expressionist Architecture
